slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Urine (clean-catch sample; 24-hour collection in some cases)

What it is used for: A urinalysis may include a visual check, tests for certain chemicals and a microscopic exam; the chemical part checks substances such as protein, glucose, ketones, bilirubin, urobilinogen and nitrites, and dipstick (test strip) methods can be used. Urinalysis is used to check general health, including the urinary tract and kidneys, and helps diagnose kidney and liver problems.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Urine ketones are used to monitor people more likely to develop high ketone levels, such as those with diabetes, long-lasting vomiting or diarrhea, alcohol use disorder, eating disorders or starvation, certain digestive diseases, a low-carbohydrate (“keto”) diet, prolonged very hard exercise, or pregnancy.

Physiology: Normally urine contains very little protein, because tiny kidney filters stop large protein molecules from passing into urine. High urine protein over time may be the first sign that kidney disease or another condition has damaged these filters, so the test can help find kidney damage early.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: High: High urine protein can be temporary, for example due to strenuous exercise, dehydration, diet, stress or pregnancy, so repeat testing may be needed. Protein that stays high is likely a sign of kidney disease or kidney damage, and more tests are needed to find the cause.

High: Normally urine contains little or no glucose because the kidneys return it to the blood. More glucose than normal may reflect high blood glucose (diabetes is the most common cause) or, rarely, a kidney condition such as renal glycosuria or Fanconi syndrome, in which glucose is removed even when blood glucose is normal. Pregnancy and gestational diabetes are also listed.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: High: Many bacteria that cause urinary tract infections (UTIs) change nitrates, a normal chemical in urine, into nitrites, so nitrites in urine usually mean a UTI.

High: When cells cannot get enough glucose, the body breaks down fat for energy, producing ketones. Some ketones in urine are normal, but high levels may indicate ketoacidosis, most commonly diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a medical emergency that often develops quickly and can be life-threatening.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: High: Bilirubin is normally not found in urine. Its presence (bilirubinuria) may be a sign of liver disease, such as hepatitis or cirrhosis, or of a blockage in the bile ducts; it can be an early sign of liver damage and may appear before symptoms do.

High: Normal urine contains some urobilinogen, which helpful gut bacteria make from bilirubin in bile. A higher-than-normal level may be a sign of hepatitis, cirrhosis, liver damage due to medicines or hemolytic anemia.

Low: Too little or no urobilinogen may be a sign of a blockage in the ducts that carry bile from the liver or gallbladder to the intestines, a blockage of blood flow through the liver, or a problem with liver function.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Because the amount of protein and other substances in urine varies during the day, a 24-hour urine collection may give more complete results.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: The sample is usually collected by the clean-catch method: after washing hands and cleaning the genital area, the first few seconds of urine go into the toilet and the rest is collected in the container without touching its inside, so that germs from the skin do not get into the sample. Bleeding hemorrhoids or a menstrual period should be reported before the test.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Fasting may be required before a urine ketone test or when other urine or blood tests are ordered. Some medicines may need to be stopped, but only on the provider’s instruction; all medicines being taken should be reported.
Urine for routine analysis is examined within 1 hour of collection, and the pH must also be tested within 1 hour. If testing is delayed, keep the sample refrigerated until it is analysed.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: What changes when urine stands: per the WHO table, glucose falls within about 2 hours both at room temperature and at 4–8 °C (bacteria consume it), and pH rises as ammonium forms, so the urine turns alkaline. The textbook lists the same changes and stresses falsely low glucose after a delay.
Urine protein is more stable: the WHO table gives 1 day at room temperature, 7 days at 4–8 °C and 1 month at −20 °C.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Interferences: Certain medicines, vitamin C and eating a large meal may affect urine glucose results.
Certain medicines and supplements can affect urine bilirubin and urobilinogen results, so everything being taken should be reported.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Bilirubin breaks down in light: the textbook says fresh urine must be shielded from sunlight and fluorescent light, because bilirubin oxidises to biliverdin, which the strip does not detect (false negative). The WHO document likewise requires darkness for serum bilirubin stored over 8 hours; it gives no separate time for urine.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) can affect the urine glucose result; the textbook lists it as a substance that lowers strip sensitivity and gives a false-negative result.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Limitations: Urine glucose testing is less accurate than blood glucose testing, so blood tests are now more commonly used to diagnose and monitor diabetes. A normal urine glucose does not exclude diabetes, because urine glucose can be normal while blood glucose is high, and a urine glucose test alone cannot diagnose any condition.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: A negative nitrite test does not exclude infection, because some bacteria do not change nitrates into nitrites; results for white blood cells in urine are also considered. Home UTI test strips may miss an infection, and a urine culture shows how much and what type of bacteria are present.

slides.title: Urine chemistry (dipstick)
bullets: Ketone results may be a number or reported as a “small”, “moderate” or “large” amount, and normal results can vary with diet, activity level and other factors.
Urine bilirubin is only one measure of liver health, and a urobilinogen test alone cannot diagnose a specific condition; abnormal results may lead to further tests such as a liver panel.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Urine (clean-catch sample; 24-hour collection in some cases)

What it is used for: The microscopic exam is the part of a urinalysis in which urine is examined under a microscope for certain types of cells, crystals and mucus. It may be part of a routine checkup or be ordered when visual or chemical urine results are abnormal or there are symptoms of a urinary or kidney disorder.

Physiology: Epithelial cells cover body surfaces, including the urinary tract. Three types line the urinary tract: transitional cells, renal (kidney) tubular cells and squamous cells; a small number of certain types in urine is normal.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Urine crystals form in the kidneys when certain minerals clump together with other substances, usually when urine has high levels of those minerals or too much or too little acid. A few small crystals are normal; large amounts of certain types may signal a condition needing treatment, and some crystals can stick together to form kidney stones.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: High: Blood in urine (hematuria) may be visible (gross hematuria) or seen only under a microscope or found by urinalysis (microscopic hematuria). Most causes are not serious, such as certain medicines, intense exercise, sexual activity or menstruation.

High: Sometimes blood in urine signals a more serious problem: infection of the bladder, kidney or prostate; bladder or kidney stones; kidney injury; a viral infection such as hepatitis; cancer of the bladder, kidney or prostate; enlarged prostate (BPH); inflammation of the kidney, urethra or bladder; a blood disorder; polycystic kidney disease; or disorders of the ureters. More tests may be needed to find the cause.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: High: Red or white blood cells in urine may in some cases mean a condition that needs treatment, such as a urinary tract infection, kidney disease or liver disease.

High: Epithelial cells are often reported as “few”, “moderate” or “many”; “few” is typically normal. Moderate or many cells may be a sign of a urinary tract infection, yeast infection, kidney disease, liver disease or certain cancers.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: High: Reports usually state whether crystals are present, their amount and what they are made of. Calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate crystals are the most common cause of kidney stones; large amounts of uric acid and urate crystals may form when metabolic problems such as gout or type 2 diabetes make urine too acidic; repeated urinary tract infections may cause large amounts of struvite crystals.

High: A small or moderate amount of mucus in urine is a normal finding. A large amount may be a sign of a urinary tract infection, a sexually transmitted infection, kidney stones, irritable bowel syndrome or bladder cancer, and more tests may be needed to find out why.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: Pre-analytics: For crystals, a clean-catch sample or a 24-hour collection may be used; the 24-hour test may be more accurate because the amount of crystals varies during the day. During collection the container is stored in a refrigerator or a cooler with ice.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: Samples are usually collected by the clean-catch method so that germs from the skin do not get into the sample; following all collection instructions carefully helps make results accurate.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: Examine urine for sediment promptly: the WHO table gives sediment stability of 1–2 hours at room temperature and 1–8 hours at 4–8 °C, and it must not be frozen. The textbook likewise requires microscopy within 1 hour of collection.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: Formed elements deteriorate with delay: the WHO table gives erythrocytes about 1 hour at room temperature (longer in concentrated urine), and the 2 days listed for casts apply only to concentrated urine (osmolality >300 mosmol/kg). The textbooks note lysis of red cells, breakdown of casts and partial destruction of cells in alkaline urine.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: Interferences: Some medicines and certain foods, such as beets or rhubarb, can also turn urine red. Blood from bleeding hemorrhoids or a menstrual period can get into the sample and affect results, so these should be reported before the test.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: Squamous epithelial cells in urine may mean the sample was contaminated with cells from another part of the body, which can happen if the genital area is not cleaned well enough during clean-catch collection.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: Crystals do not always mean a condition that needs treatment: large amounts of some types may be caused by certain medicines (calcium-based antacids, some antibiotics, diuretics, antiviral medicines), a diet with too much animal protein (fish, shellfish, organ meats) or not drinking enough fluids.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy
bullets: Limitations: An abnormal microscopic finding does not always mean a condition that needs treatment; more tests may be needed before a diagnosis can be made.

Refrigerated urine may contain excess precipitated salts and be unsuitable for microscopy. For microscopy, urine can be preserved with 10% formaldehyde (8–10 drops per 300 ml), but it is then unsuitable for other tests.

slides.title: Urine culture
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Midstream clean-catch urine in a sterile cup, or a catheter sample
What it is used for: Ordered for symptoms of a urinary tract or bladder infection, such as pain or burning when urinating. It may also be done after treatment to make sure all the bacteria are gone.

Physiology: The laboratory determines which bacteria or yeast, if any, are in the urine; this takes 24 to 48 hours. To find which antibiotic will work, the organism is tested against different antibiotics (sensitivity testing).

slides.title: Urine culture
cols: A positive result means bacteria or yeast were found, which likely means a urinary tract or bladder infection. Other tests show which organism it is and which antibiotics will work best, if treatment is needed. Sometimes more than one type of bacteria, or only a small amount, is found.
"Normal growth" is a normal result and means there is no infection.

slides.title: Urine culture
cols: Sensitivity results: susceptible (the antibiotic stopped or killed the organism), intermediate (it may work at a higher or more frequent dose), resistant (it did not work and is not a good choice).

slides.title: Urine culture
bullets: Pre-analytics: If possible, collect urine that has been in the bladder for 2–3 hours. Wash hands with soap. Women wipe the inner labia front to back, then the urethral opening with a second wipe; men clean the head of the penis. Pass a small amount into the toilet, stop the flow, then collect urine until the cup is about half full and finish in the toilet.

slides.title: Urine culture
bullets: Do not touch the inside of the cup or lid, close it tightly, and if at home put it in a plastic bag in the refrigerator.
A sample can also be taken with a thin catheter passed through the urethra into the bladder, or rarely with a needle through the lower abdomen into the bladder.

slides.title: Urine culture
bullets: Collect urine for culture into a sterile container, if possible before antibiotics start, and deliver it quickly: per the WHO table bacteria multiply within 1–2 hours at room temperature but stay stable for about 24 hours at 4–8 °C. The textbook likewise gives 1–2 hours, or up to 24 hours refrigerated.
Interferences: Taking antibiotics can cause a false-negative urine culture.

slides.title: Urine culture
bullets: Limitations: Normal value ranges may vary slightly between laboratories, and some labs use different measurements or test different samples. Sometimes more than one type of bacteria, or only a small amount, is found in the culture; the provider explains what a specific result means.

slides.title: 24-hour urine collection
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: All urine passed over 24 hours (kept cool)  ·  Units: mL/24 h, mg/24 h

What it is used for: Ordered when blood, urine or imaging tests show signs of reduced kidney function. Urine volume is usually measured as part of tests of substances passed in a day — creatinine, sodium, potassium, urea nitrogen and protein. It is also done for polyuria, such as in diabetes insipidus.

slides.title: 24-hour urine collection
bullets: Example reference interval from the source (not your laboratory’s interval): 24-hour urine volume — 800–2,000 mL/24 h with a fluid intake of about 2 litres a day. MedlinePlus notes that normal ranges vary between laboratories — compare your result with your laboratory’s own reference interval.

Lower 24-hour urine volume: dehydration, low fluid intake, some types of chronic kidney disease. Higher volume: renal or central diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, high fluid intake, some kidney diseases and diuretic medicines.

slides.title: 24-hour urine collection
bullets: Example reference interval from the source (not your laboratory’s interval): 24-hour urine protein — less than 100 mg/24 h (as a urine concentration, less than 10 mg/dL). Laboratories may use different measurements or samples — compare your result with your laboratory’s own reference interval.

Raised 24-hour protein: amyloidosis, bladder tumor, heart failure, preeclampsia, kidney disease from diabetes, high blood pressure, autoimmune and other causes, and multiple myeloma. Healthy people may have higher protein after strenuous exercise or dehydration.

slides.title: 24-hour urine collection
bullets: Pre-analytics: On day 1, urinate into the toilet when you get up. After that, collect all urine in a special container for the next 24 hours. On day 2, urinate into the container when you get up, exactly 24 hours after starting. Cap the container, keep it in the refrigerator or a cool place during collection, label it with name, date and completion time, and deliver it as soon as possible. For infants, an adhesive urine collection bag is used.

slides.title: 24-hour urine collection
bullets: Collect 24-hour urine into a clean container of at least 2 litres: discard the first morning void and include the next morning’s first void. Keep the container at 4–8 °C during collection; if analysis is delayed beyond 24 hours, store the specimen at −20 °C. The laboratory measures and records the total volume.

slides.title: 24-hour urine collection
bullets: Interferences: Results can be affected by certain medicines (never stop one without asking), dehydration, an x-ray with contrast dye within 3 days before, severe emotional stress, vaginal fluid getting into the urine, strenuous exercise and urinary tract infection.

slides.title: 24-hour urine collection
bullets: Limitations: To avoid a 24-hour collection, the provider may order a protein-to-creatinine ratio on a single (random) urine sample instead. This is a different test: it gives the ratio of protein to creatinine, not the amount passed in 24 hours. Normal ranges vary between laboratories — discuss your result with your provider.

slides.title: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Urine (random, early-morning/timed or 24-hour)  ·  Units: mg/g

What it is used for: Most often used to look for signs of kidney disease in high-risk people without symptoms (diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, family history, age over 50, smoking, obesity) and to monitor diagnosed kidney disease and its treatment. Because diabetes is the most common cause of kidney disease, people with diabetes should be tested every year.

slides.title: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Albumin is a common blood protein, not a waste product, so very little should pass into urine: healthy kidney filters let through at most a trace (often called microalbumin), whereas damaged kidneys may let larger amounts pass. Abnormal urine albumin may be an early sign of kidney disease.

Creatinine, a waste product of daily muscle wear, is usually excreted by the kidneys at a steady rate. Comparing urine albumin with creatinine therefore shows whether albumin is being lost at an increased rate.

UACR = urine albumin (mg/dL) ÷ urine creatinine (g/dL), expressed in mg/g, which approximates albumin excretion in mg/day. Unlike a dipstick test for albumin, UACR is unaffected by variation in urine concentration.

slides.title: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · Reference values and decision limits · 1/2
rows: People tested for kidney disease (NIDDK; the quick reference applies it to patients with diabetes) — More than 30 mg/g (30 mg/g or less is described as normal). If albumin is found, the test is usually repeated once or twice to confirm.

slides.title: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
slides.eyebrow: Urinalysis · Reference values and decision limits · 2/2
rows: Patients with diabetes evaluated for kidney disease (NIDDK quick reference) — Older term for urine albumin levels not detected by a dipstick test.
Patients with diabetes evaluated for kidney disease (NIDDK quick reference) — More than 300 mg/g; the source describes the term as “sometimes used”.

slides.title: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
bullets: High: Higher or increasing urine albumin usually means more serious kidney disease that is likely to get worse faster, and a higher risk of heart and blood vessel disease. Smaller amounts do not always mean kidney disease.

slides.title: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
bullets: Pre-analytics: The sample may be a random (spot) urine, an early-morning or timed urine (first thing in the morning or after 4 hours without urinating), or a 24-hour collection. MedlinePlus calls the 24-hour collection the most accurate way to measure urine albumin, while NIDDK’s diabetes quick reference recommends a spot UACR and says 24-hour and timed specimens are not necessary.

Before the sample, the person may need to avoid intense exercise, which can briefly increase urine albumin, and may be asked not to eat meat for a day because meat can affect the result. Ask the provider whether any medicines or supplements could affect it.

slides.title: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
bullets: Interferences: Temporary increases in urine albumin can be caused by exercise, certain medicines, fever and inflammation; inflammatory conditions such as urinary tract infection, gum infection (periodontitis) and hepatitis can also raise it. Results may also be affected by muscle density, diet, age and race.

Limitations: An abnormal result needs confirmation: usually two more tests are done within 3–6 months, and early-stage kidney disease is possible if two of three are abnormal. An eGFR blood test is usually ordered as well.
Albumin should not be confused with prealbumin: prealbumin is a different protein, and a prealbumin test is not part of kidney testing.

slides.title: Example: Nechiporenko count
bullets: Formula: x (per 1 µL of sediment) = A ÷ V, where A is the cells counted and V the volume of the ruling counted, µL. N (per 1 ml of urine) = x × sediment volume (µL) ÷ urine centrifuged (ml) [1, p. 44].
slides.ex: Example (Aripova [2, p. 99]): 10 ml urine, 1 ml sediment, 100 large Goryaev squares (0.4 µL) → N = A × 250.

slides.title: A first UACR is abnormal; the sample was collected the day after a hard workout, during a fever. What is the appropriate next step per the source?
options: Confirm with repeat tests—usually two more within 3–6 months; early kidney disease is possible if two of three are abnormal.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source describes exactly this confirmation approach.

Basis: MedlinePlus: exercise, medicines, fever and inflammation can cause temporary increases; usually two more tests are done within 3–6 months.

slides.title: Why is albumin expressed relative to creatinine in a spot urine sample?
options: Because creatinine is a breakdown product of albumin.
Because the ratio makes confirmation testing unnecessary.
Creatinine is usually excreted at a steady rate, so the ratio is unaffected by urine concentration and estimates 24-hour albumin excretion.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: consistent with MedlinePlus and NIDDK.

Basis: NIDDK: UACR estimates 24-hour albumin excretion and, unlike a dipstick, is unaffected by urine concentration; MedlinePlus: creatinine is usually excreted at a steady rate.

slides.title: A patient with UTI symptoms has a negative urine nitrite test. Which interpretation follows the source?
options: A negative nitrite fully rules out a UTI
Infection is still possible because some bacteria do not change nitrates into nitrites; white blood cell results are also considered
A negative nitrite indicates kidney disease
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source describes exactly this limitation and the need to look at white blood cells in urine.

Basis: The nitrite test relies on bacteria changing nitrates into nitrites; bacteria that do not do this give a negative result despite infection.

slides.title: A large amount of protein is found in the urine of a person who ran a marathon the day before. Which approach follows the source?
options: Diagnose chronic kidney disease from this single result, because a large amount of protein in urine is never a temporary finding
Ignore it, because protein in urine after exercise is always harmless and needs no follow-up
Recognize that strenuous exercise can raise urine protein for a short time and check on repeat testing whether it persists
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source lists strenuous exercise as a cause of a short-term rise and suggests repeat urinalysis to see whether protein stays high.

Basis: Urine protein can rise temporarily; it is persistently high protein that points to kidney disease.

slides.title: A urine microscopy report shows many squamous epithelial cells. What should be considered first, according to the source?
options: The sample may be contaminated, e.g. the genital area was not cleaned well during clean-catch collection
It confirms kidney disease, so no repeat sample or further tests are needed
Squamous cells are the same as kidney tubular cells, so a large number of them means the tubules are damaged
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source says squamous epithelial cells in urine may mean the sample was contaminated.

Basis: Many squamous cells may reflect how the sample was collected.

slides.title: A routine urinalysis shows a few small crystals. Which interpretation fits the source?
options: Any crystals mean kidney stones are present
A few small crystals are normal; large amounts of certain types may signal a condition, and medicines, diet or low fluid intake can also increase crystals
Crystals are not influenced by diet or fluid intake
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. This is how the source describes it.

Basis: A few small crystals are normal; large amounts are interpreted in context.

Theory of urine formation?
bullets: 1. Urine is formed in the nephron: filtration in the glomeruli (primary urine – protein-free ultrafiltrate of plasma, ~180 L per day), reabsorption and secretion in the tubules, concentration in the collecting ducts.
2. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the main indicator of kidney function; in practice eGFR is calculated from creatinine (and cystatin C).

3. Proximal tubule: glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate, Na and most of the water are reabsorbed; loop of Henle – concentration gradient via the countercurrent mechanism; distal tubule and collecting ducts – final regulation under aldosterone (Na/K) and ADH (water).

slides.title: Theory of urine formation?
bullets: 4. Laboratory reflection: glucosuria (if filtered glucose exceeds reabsorption capacity), proteinuria (glomerular or tubular damage), urine density/osmolality (concentrating ability).
5. Kidney disease is classified by KDIGO by eGFR (G1–G5) and albuminuria (A1–A3).

slides.title: Examining the physical and chemical properties of urine?
bullets: 1. Physical properties: amount (in adults ~600–2000 mL/day), color (bilirubin, blood, hemoglobin/myoglobin, drugs), clarity (turbidity – salts, leukocytes, bacteria, mucus), odor, relative density (1.002–1.035; urinometer, refractometer or test strip) – renal concentrating ability.

2. Chemical examination – test strips: pH (4.5–8), protein (mainly albumin; alkaline pH – false positive), glucose (when the reabsorption threshold is exceeded), ketones (acetoacetate/acetone, β-hydroxybutyrate is not detected), blood (erythrocytes, hemoglobin, myoglobin – peroxidase activity), leukocyte esterase, nitrites (some bacteria), bilirubin, urobilinogen.

slides.title: Examining the physical and chemical properties of urine?
bullets: 3. Interferences: ascorbate (false negative blood, glucose, nitrite, leukocyte esterase), concentrated or dilute urine, drugs (phenazopyridine).
4. Confirmatory tests: for protein – sulfosalicylic acid (all proteins) and quantitative UPCR/ACR, for blood – microscopy, glucose and ketones in blood.
5. Preanalytics: midstream, morning urine, analysis within 1 hour or storage at 4 °C.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy?
bullets: 1. Preparation: 5–12 mL of well-mixed fresh urine, centrifuged at ~400×g for 5 minutes, resuspended in a standard volume; under a coverslip at low (×100) and high (×400) magnification; phase contrast/staining, polarization for crystals.

2. Organized elements: erythrocytes (normal 0–5/field; dysmorphic erythrocytes and acanthocytes – glomerular source), leukocytes (0–5; many – infection, inflammation), epithelium (squamous, transitional, renal tubular), casts.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy?
bullets: 3. Casts: hyaline (a few are normal; concentrated urine, exertion), erythrocyte (glomerulonephritis, vasculitis), leukocyte (pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis), granular (tubular damage), waxy (severe CKD), fatty (nephrotic syndrome).
4. Unorganized elements: crystals (oxalates, urates, uric acid, triple phosphates – infection; cystine – cystinuria), bacteria, fungi, trichomonads, sperm.
5. Automated urine particle analyzers (flow cytometry, digital imaging) – screening; abnormal results are confirmed by microscopy; the result is standardized per unit volume (/µL).
